issues.legal_issue: A karta may execute an agreement to sell joint Hindu family property without the signatures of the other coparceners.
material_facts: The property was accepted to be joint Hindu family property.
The karta executed the agreement to sell, which was also signed by his wife and the family’s father-in-law; the son did not sign it.
The agreement stated that the executants were selling the property because they needed funds for domestic necessities.
issues.conclusion: The karta was entitled to execute the agreement to sell, and the son’s missing signature did not invalidate it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sri Narayan Bal v. Sridhar Sutar and Kehar Singh v. Nachittar Kaur, a joint Hindu family may act through its karta in managing family property. A karta may alienate family property for legal necessity or the benefit of the estate, and such an alienation binds the family. The karta has discretion in assessing necessity, which depends on the facts of each case; Mulla on Hindu Law, Articles 240, 241 and 254, describes family necessities and the karta’s powers.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and joint_family_property and agreement_executed_by_karta and coparcener_did_not_sign

predicates.specific_performance_case: A party seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.joint_family_property: The property is held as joint Hindu family property.
predicates.agreement_executed_by_karta: The karta executed the agreement to sell the family property.
predicates.coparcener_did_not_sign: A coparcener did not sign the agreement to sell.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim concerns joint Hindu family property and the karta executed the agreement, a coparcener’s failure to sign does not by itself invalidate the agreement.

issues.legal_issue: The stated need for family funds and the need to clear a debt secured on family property can establish legal necessity for an agreement to sell.
material_facts: The agreement stated that the executants needed funds for domestic necessities.
The respondents pleaded that the family needed funds.
The property was mortgaged to a bank, and the executants had stated that the bank dues would be cleared to release the mortgage before registration of the sale.
issues.conclusion: The agreement could not be set aside for lack of legal necessity; the circumstances established legal necessity in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Kehar Singh v. Nachittar Kaur, referring to Mulla on Hindu Law, Articles 240 and 241, recognizes maintenance of family members and payment of debts payable out of family property among possible family necessities. The listed necessities are not exhaustive; whether legal necessity exists depends on the facts of the case, and the karta has wide discretion in deciding how to meet it.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and family_need_for_funds_stated and family_property_encumbered and sale_intended_to_clear_family_debt

predicates.specific_performance_case: A party seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.family_need_for_funds_stated: The family’s need for funds was stated by the executants or acknowledged by the opposing side.
predicates.family_property_encumbered: The family property was subject to a debt or other encumbrance.
predicates.sale_intended_to_clear_family_debt: The proposed sale was intended to clear a debt secured on the family property.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim involves a stated family need for funds, encumbered family property and a sale intended to clear the family debt, those circumstances can support a finding of legal necessity.

issues.legal_issue: Omitting an issue from the trial court’s framed issues does not invalidate the trial when the parties understood the dispute and presented evidence on it.
material_facts: The trial court did not frame an issue on the karta’s authority to execute the agreement or on legal necessity.
The parties knew the opposing positions and led evidence supporting their respective contentions and refuting the other side’s contentions.
issues.conclusion: The omission of an issue did not vitiate the trial.
issues.legal_principle: Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not require a trial to be vitiated for an omitted issue where the parties went to trial fully aware of the rival cases and led evidence on them. The Court relied on Kannan v. V.S. Pandurangam and Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao.

rule.if: civil_trial_case and issue_not_framed and parties_understood_rival_cases and evidence_led_on_issue

predicates.civil_trial_case: The matter was tried in a civil court.
predicates.issue_not_framed: The trial court did not frame an issue on a matter later relied on in deciding the dispute.
predicates.parties_understood_rival_cases: Both sides understood the opposing positions on that matter.
predicates.evidence_led_on_issue: The parties presented evidence supporting or refuting those positions.

issues.definition: In a civil trial, omission of an issue does not invalidate the trial when the parties understood the dispute and presented evidence on it.

issues.legal_issue: The rule concerning an agreement executed by only some heirs of property inherited on intestacy does not govern an agreement executed by the karta of joint Hindu family property.
material_facts: The property in this case was joint Hindu family property, and the agreement was executed by the karta.

The High Court relied on Pemmada Prabhakar, which concerned property inherited on intestacy by Class I heirs under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act and an agreement not signed by some of those heirs.
issues.conclusion: Pemmada Prabhakar did not apply because it concerned inherited property and not joint Hindu family property.
issues.legal_principle: Pemmada Prabhakar v. Youngmen’s Vysya Association concerned property inherited by Class I heirs under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act; an agreement not signed by some heirs was not binding or enforceable against those non-executants. That reasoning does not govern joint Hindu family property, which may be dealt with by its karta in accordance with the rules governing karta authority and legal necessity.

predicates.joint_family_property: The property is held as joint Hindu family property.
predicates.agreement_executed_by_karta: The karta executed the agreement to sell the family property.
predicates.nonexecutant_heir_precedent_relied_on: A party relies on a rule concerning an agreement made by some, but not all, heirs of property inherited on intestacy.

issues.definition: When a karta executed an agreement concerning joint Hindu family property, a rule about agreements by some heirs of inherited property does not control the dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of disputed property made while litigation concerning its sale is pending remains subject to the outcome of that litigation.
material_facts: The property was transferred to a third person during the pendency of the appeal.
The Court restored the decree for specific performance and directed performance of the obligations under the agreement notwithstanding the later transfer.
issues.conclusion: The later transfer was subject to the doctrine of lis pendens, and the respondents remained bound to perform the agreement notwithstanding that transfer.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of lis pendens makes a transfer of property during pending litigation subject to the result of that litigation. The Court applied that doctrine to the transfer made during the appeal.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: An appeal concerns a claim for specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.property_transferred_during_pending_liti: The disputed property was transferred to another person while the litigation was pending.

issues.definition: When disputed property is transferred during an appeal concerning its sale, the transfer remains subject to the outcome of that litigation.
